title: COME AS YOU ARE—BUT DON’T ASK JESUS TO LEAVE YOU THAT WAY
paragraphs: COME AS YOU ARE—BUT DON’T ASK JESUS TO LEAVE YOU THAT WAY
The invitation of Jesus is more gracious than religion told you—and far more transforming than modern Christianity sometimes admits.
There is a sentence Christians love to say:
“Come as you are.”
It sounds beautiful.
It sounds like grace.
And, understood correctly, it is.
But there is something Jesus never said:
“Come as you are, stay as you are, protect everything that is destroying you, rename your chains freedom, and ask Me to bless the life I came to redeem.”
That is not grace.
And somewhere, somebody reading this already knows why this matters.
Because maybe you have been using the kindness of Jesus as permission to keep negotiating with the very thing that is killing your soul.
Maybe nobody knows.
You still post the verses.
You still say, “God is good.”
You still know when to lift your hands.
You still know Christian language well enough that nobody suspects the war happening behind your smile.
But there is a door you keep reopening.
A conversation you know you should end.
A browser history you keep deleting.
A bitterness you keep feeding.
A relationship you keep defending.
A secret compromise you have learned to call “struggling” because admitting that you have stopped fighting would hurt too much.
And perhaps you have whispered to yourself:
Jesus accepts me as I am.
Yes.
But listen carefully, because this may be the sentence you remember long after you forget the rest of this article:
Jesus receives sinners exactly where He finds them, but His grace loves them too much to make peace with what is destroying them.
That distinction changes everything.
The popular expression “come as you are” is not a direct Bible quotation. Scripture gives us something even better.
Jesus actually says:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” — Matthew 11:28, KJV
The Greek begins:
Δεῦτε πρός με — Deute pros me.
“Come to Me.”
That matters.
The invitation is not merely, Come.
It has a destination.
Me.
Jesus Christ Himself.
The Greek word δεῦτε (deute) carries the force of an invitation or summons: “come here,” “come!” Matthew 11:28 uses δεῦτε πρός με—come to Me.
Christianity is therefore not primarily an invitation to become more comfortable with yourself.
It is an invitation to Christ.
Come filthy.
Come ashamed.
Come addicted.
Come angry.
Come sexually broken.
Come religious.
Come self-righteous.
Come exhausted.
Come confused.
Come after the divorce.
Come after the relapse.
Come after the secret nobody knows.
Come after you promised God you would never do it again—and did.
Come when your prayers sound pathetic to you.
Come when you cannot remember the last time you opened your Bible without feeling guilty.
Come when you have wasted years.
Come when you feel too dirty to say His name.
Come.
But come to Jesus.
That last part changes the entire invitation.

Because the Jesus who says, “Come to Me,” immediately continues by speaking about taking His yoke and learning from Him. His invitation to rest is therefore not an invitation to autonomous spirituality; it is an invitation into relationship, discipleship, and submission to Christ.
Grace says you do not have to clean yourself before approaching Jesus.
Repentance says you cannot encounter Jesus while insisting that He never touch your dirt.
Do you see the difference?
Imagine a man drowning in the ocean.
A rescuer reaches down from a boat and screams, “Give me your hand!”
Would anyone call the rescuer hateful because he refuses to affirm the drowning man's present condition?
Of course not.
The urgency exists precisely because the rescuer values his life.
That is closer to the Gospel.
We were not merely imperfect people needing encouragement.
We were sinners needing reconciliation with God.
And God did not wait for humanity to become impressive enough to deserve rescue.
Christ came for sinners.
The cross is not God's declaration that sin does not matter.
The cross is the terrifying evidence that sin matters—and the breathtaking evidence that sinners matter to God.
Look at Jesus.
Really look at Him.
He touched people others avoided.
He ate with people respectable society despised.
He welcomed the broken.
He showed mercy to the guilty.
He confronted hypocrites.
He received desperate people who had nothing impressive to bring Him.
But nowhere does the mercy of Jesus become approval of sin.
Jesus did not need sinners to become righteous before approaching Him.
If they could accomplish that themselves, they would not need a Savior.
But neither did He die and rise again merely to make sinners comfortable remaining enslaved.
This is where our generation can confuse acceptance with affirmation.
They are not identical.
A doctor can receive you compassionately without affirming your cancer.
A firefighter can carry you lovingly without affirming the flames.
And Jesus can receive you completely without calling your chains jewelry.
In fact, sometimes the most loving thing Christ does is expose what we have spent years hiding.
That hurts.
Ask Peter.
Peter once sounded fearless.
He was the disciple who insisted he would remain faithful.
Then came the courtyard.
Pressure.
Fear.
Questions.
And three denials.
Then the rooster.
There are moments in Scripture that almost seem to have sound.
That rooster is one of them.
Imagine hearing it.
Imagine remembering what Jesus had said.
Imagine realizing that the version of yourself you confidently advertised was not the person who appeared under pressure.
Peter broke.
Yet his failure was not the end of his story.
After the resurrection, Jesus restored him and recommissioned him.
Peter's scandal did not get the final sentence.
Grace did.
But notice what grace did not do.
Jesus did not meet Peter and say, “Denial is simply who you are. Embrace it.”
He restored him.
Called him.
Commissioned him.
Changed the direction of his life.
That is grace.
Grace does not merely sit beside your grave and tell you that death is acceptable.
Grace calls you out of it.
And perhaps that is why this message feels uncomfortable.
Because many of us want a Savior from consequences without wanting a Lord over desires.
We want forgiveness without surrender.
Comfort without correction.
Heaven without holiness.
A cross without dying to self.
A Jesus who follows us instead of a Jesus we follow.
But biblical Christianity does not offer Jesus as an accessory to the life we have already decided to live.
He is Lord.
And the scandalous beauty is that this Lord welcomes people who have absolutely no business boasting before Him.
Listen to another promise from Jesus:
“him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” — John 6:37, KJV
The Greek is extraordinarily strong:
τὸν ἐρχόμενον πρός με οὐ μὴ ἐκβάλω ἔξω
The expression οὐ μὴ gives emphatic force to the denial. The one coming to Christ will certainly not be cast out.
Think about that.
You may be ashamed to come.
Come anyway.
You may have failed again.
Come anyway.
You may be carrying consequences you cannot undo.
Come anyway.
You may have prayed the same repentance prayer so many times that you wonder whether heaven is tired of hearing your voice.
Come to Christ.
Do not confuse conviction with rejection.
The Savior who exposes sin is also the Savior who receives sinners.
You do not need to wait until you feel worthy.
You will never make yourself worthy enough to turn Calvary into wages.
Salvation is grace.
The blood of Christ is not a paycheck for well-behaved people.
Jesus came to save sinners.
But when grace gets hold of a human being, something begins happening.
Not instant perfection.
Transformation.
Sometimes slow.
Sometimes painful.
Sometimes involving relapse, tears, accountability, confession, getting back up, apologizing, cutting things off, returning to Scripture, and learning obedience one trembling decision at a time.
The Christian life is not sinless perfection.
But neither is it peaceful surrender to sin.
There is a difference between falling in battle and making your home in the enemy's camp.
One says:
“Jesus, I fell again. Help me.”
The other eventually says:
“Jesus, stop calling this a fall.”
That is where “come as you are” can become dangerous when detached from repentance.
The Gospel says:
Come without pretending.
Come without cleaning yourself first.
Come without manufacturing righteousness.
Come without a résumé.
Come without excuses.
Come because Christ is sufficient.
And then trust Him enough to let Him begin dismantling what sin built inside you.
Some things will have to die.
Some numbers may need deleting.
Some relationships may need boundaries.
Some habits will have to be confessed.
Some pride will have to break.
Some apologies will need to be made.
Some secret rooms will need light.
Some idols will have to fall.
And yes...
sometimes following Jesus will cost you something you desperately wanted to keep.
But whatever Christ asks you to surrender cannot compare with Christ Himself.
That is what repentance is so often misunderstood to mean.
Repentance is not paying God back.
You cannot.
Repentance is not making yourself clean enough for grace.
You cannot.
Repentance is the turning of the sinner toward God, inseparable from genuine faith in Christ. When Jesus began proclaiming the Gospel, His message included the command to repent and believe.
Christianity is not:
“Fix yourself, then come.”
Neither is Christianity:
“Come, and never change.”
It is:
“Come to Christ—and let Christ become Lord of everything.”
That means you can walk into His presence carrying yesterday's shame.
But you do not have to carry it back out as your identity.
Your sin may explain parts of your history.
It does not have authority to name your eternity.
Your worst night may be part of your testimony.
It does not have to become your destiny.
The cross proves that Jesus takes sin more seriously than we do.
The resurrection proves that sin and death do not get the last word.
This is why Gospel grace is simultaneously devastating and beautiful.
It destroys boasting.
The moral person cannot boast.
The addict cannot despair.
The religious person cannot claim superiority.
The prodigal cannot claim hopelessness.
Everybody comes through the same bloodstained door.
Jesus.
Maybe you have spent years believing you need to hide the ugliest part of yourself from God.
You cannot shock the One who already knows.
The secret you are terrified to confess is not new information to Him.
The question is not whether He knows.
The question is whether you will finally stop hiding.
Imagine standing before Christ with your fists clenched around the very chain He died to break.
And imagine Him saying:
“Come.”
Not because the chain is harmless.
Because He is stronger than the chain.
That changes the way we understand holiness too.
Holiness is not God ruining your fun.
Holiness is God reclaiming what sin has vandalized.
Purity is not punishment.
Freedom is not deprivation.
Obedience is not God stealing your life.
Jesus came that sinners might be reconciled to God and receive life in Him.
And sometimes what feels like God taking something away is actually God refusing to let something else take you away.
Read that again.
Maybe the relationship you keep begging Him to preserve is destroying your obedience.
Maybe the habit you call harmless has quietly become your master.
Maybe your resentment feels justified because forgiveness feels like surrender.
Maybe your secret life has become so normal that conviction now feels offensive.
Maybe you are not waiting for God's answer anymore.
Maybe you are waiting for Him to agree with yours.
And He loves you too much for that.
There is mercy in His “no.”
There is mercy in conviction.
There is mercy when Scripture interrupts you.
There is mercy when the sermon feels uncomfortably specific.
There is mercy when your excuses stop working.
There is even mercy in the moment you finally see yourself clearly.
Because conviction is not meant to make you run from Jesus.
It should drive you to Jesus.
This is where some Christians make the opposite mistake.
They speak about repentance so harshly that wounded people begin believing Jesus is disgusted by anyone who has not cleaned themselves up.
That is not the Gospel either.
Jesus is not standing at the finish line shouting, “Become righteous enough to reach Me.”
Christ came to save.
So if you are reading this while carrying something ugly...
Come.
If you slept with someone you should not have...
Come.
If pornography has been controlling you...
Come.
If anger has poisoned your home...
Come.
If money became your god...
Come.
If religion made you proud...
Come.
If church hurt left you suspicious...
Come.
If you walked away...
Come.
If you are the person everybody thinks is strong while privately you are collapsing...
Come.
But come ready to tell the truth.
Not because truth earns salvation.
Because you no longer need lies in the presence of a Savior who already knows you.
There is a strange freedom in finally saying:
“Jesus, this is me.”
Not the Instagram version.
Not the Sunday version.
Not the version your family thinks exists.
Me.
The jealous me.
The lustful me.
The bitter me.
The frightened me.
The controlling me.
The exhausted me.
The hypocritical me.
The addicted me.
The angry me.
The me who wants You and still keeps reaching for things that wound my relationship with You.
Here I am.
And Christianity's answer is not:
“Wonderful. Stay exactly there.”
The answer is:
Now follow Him.
Follow Him when obedience feels expensive.
Follow Him when feelings disappear.
Follow Him when temptation returns.
Follow Him when people mock the new boundaries.
Follow Him when your old life starts calling.
Follow Him when repentance requires admitting you were wrong.
Follow Him when nobody applauds.
Follow Him because Christianity is not merely agreeing that Jesus exists.
It is belonging to Jesus Christ.
And when you stumble?
Run back.
When you fail?
Confess.
When you are weak?
Ask for help.
When shame says, “Hide”?
Remember Eden.
Hiding is old.
Grace calls sinners into the light.
The enemy wants your failure to become your identity.
Jesus can turn failure into testimony.
The enemy says:
“Look what you did.”
The Gospel says:
“Look what Christ has done.”
The enemy says:
“You are too dirty.”
Jesus says:
“Come to Me.”
The enemy says:
“You have failed too many times.”
Jesus says of the one coming to Him that He will not cast that person out.
So come as you are.
Absolutely.
Come with tears on your face.
Come trembling.
Come skeptical.
Come exhausted.
Come guilty.
Come spiritually numb.
Come with questions.
Come after years away.
Come before you have solved yourself.
Just do not mistake the doorway for the destination.
Jesus receives you where you are so that He can make you His.
And perhaps today your response does not need to be dramatic.
Maybe it is simply:
“Jesus, no more hiding.”
Not as performance.
As confession.
There are believers who understand what it means to fight battles nobody else sees.
You do not have to pretend here.
And if this article brought someone to mind, do not merely think about them.
Not to embarrass them.
Because sometimes God puts a person on your heart because they need to be reminded that the door to Christ is still open.
Not as a religious badge.
That distinction matters.
We will never sell grace.
We will never put forgiveness behind a paywall.
Jesus already paid the price we could never pay.
More importantly, stay because you want to grow.
Because temptation has a strange way of making us forget what conviction made painfully clear.
Come back to these words when shame tells you to hide.
Share them when somebody else needs the reminder.
But before you leave, understand the heart of everything you have just read.
Jesus is not waiting for a prettier version of you.
He is not asking you to wash before approaching the fountain.
He is not demanding that the dead resurrect themselves before coming to the Resurrection and the Life.
Come bankrupt.
Come broken.
Come exposed.
Come with nothing in your hands except your need.
But when Christ reaches for your chains...
do not call them your identity and beg Him to leave them on.
The Savior who says “Come” is the Savior worth following.
The hands that receive sinners are scarred hands.
The One calling you away from sin is the One who went to the cross for sinners.
And the empty tomb means your story does not have to end where your shame says it does.
Your scandal may explain how you arrived here.
Your wounds may explain why you limp.
Your failures may occupy pages you wish you could tear out.
But if your life is surrendered to Jesus Christ, none of those things deserves the final sentence.
Come as you are—because Jesus already knows who is coming. Then stay close enough to Him that grace teaches you not to remain who you were.
That is the invitation.
That is repentance.
That is mercy.
That is hope.
That is the Gospel.
And this is the line I hope follows you long after you close this article:
Jesus did not walk into your darkness merely to sit beside your chains—He came to bring you home.
